prompt: What is the difference between `CREATE USER bruno` and `CREATE ROLE bruno`?
hint: Look at what `\du` printed beside `reporting`.

choices.text: Only LOGIN: CREATE USER switches it on and CREATE ROLE leaves it off
choices.why: Right. `CREATE USER` is `CREATE ROLE` with `LOGIN` switched on; nothing else differs.

choices.text: `CREATE USER` also makes an account in /etc/passwd
choices.why: The server never touches the operating system's accounts. `id bruno` still said no such user.

choices.text: A user belongs to one database and a role to the cluster
choices.why: Both are the same object, stored in `pg_authid`, which every database shares.

choices.text: A user gets a password and a role cannot have one
choices.why: Neither statement sets a password, and any role can be given one with `\password`.

prompt: `bruno` was created while connected to `shop`. A colleague connects to the database `ana` and runs `SELECT rolname FROM pg_roles`. Is `bruno` in the result?
hint: Which catalogue table holds roles, and is it per database?

choices.text: No, roles exist only in the database they were created in
choices.why: That is how tables behave. `pg_authid` has `relisshared` true: one copy for the whole cluster.

choices.text: Only after `GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE ana TO bruno`
choices.why: `CONNECT` decides whether bruno may log in to `ana`, not whether the role is visible there.

choices.text: Only if the colleague is a superuser, because pg_roles is hidden
choices.why: `pg_roles` is readable by everybody; it is `pg_authid`, with the passwords, that only a superuser reads.

choices.text: Yes, because a role is stored once for the whole cluster and every database sees it
choices.why: Right. Roles are cluster-wide; only what a role may do inside each database is per database.

prompt: Match each engine to what an account is there.
hint: One of them keys an account by where it connects from.

pairs.right: A role, with LOGIN or without, for the whole cluster
A name and a host together, so one name can be two accounts
A login at the server, mapped to a user in each database
A user that is also a schema for its objects

prompt: An analyst is leaving next week, but the tables he created must stay. Which statement stops him from connecting today without touching what he owns?
hint: Every attribute has a NO form.

choices.text: `DROP ROLE` him and recreate the tables
choices.why: The server refuses to drop a role that owns objects, and recreating tables is a migration, not an account change.

choices.text: `REVOKE ALL ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public FROM him`
choices.why: That removes table privileges; he could still log in, and an owner keeps every right on his own tables anyway.

choices.text: `ALTER ROLE ... NOINHERIT`
choices.why: That changes how he uses his groups' privileges, not whether he can connect.

choices.text: `ALTER ROLE ... NOLOGIN`, which closes the door
choices.why: Right. The role and everything it owns stay; only the door closes.

prompt: On PostgreSQL 16, the role `steward` has `CREATEROLE` and tries `ALTER ROLE bruno CREATEDB`, where `bruno` was created by `ana`. What happens?
hint: What did the DETAIL line ask for?

choices.text: Refused: no ADMIN option on bruno
choices.why: Right. steward has ADMIN only on the roles it created itself.

choices.text: It works: CREATEROLE manages every role that is not a superuser
choices.why: That was version 15 and earlier. Since 16 it needs the ADMIN option on that role.

choices.text: It works, but only until the next restart
choices.why: Role attributes are stored in the catalogue and survive restarts; nothing about this is temporary.

choices.text: Refused, because only a superuser may run ALTER ROLE at all
choices.why: steward could alter `intern`, the role it created. The rule is about ADMIN, not about being a superuser.

prompt: You inherit a PostgreSQL 13 server where a support account has `CREATEROLE` and nothing else. How worried should you be?
hint: Before 16, what could CREATEROLE grant?

choices.text: Not at all: it can only create new roles
choices.why: On 15 and earlier it could also alter other roles and grant membership in any role.

choices.text: A little: it can rename other people's roles
choices.why: Renaming is the least of it. Granting itself a role that runs programs on the server is the problem.

choices.text: Not at all, because version 13 has no CREATEROLE
choices.why: CREATEROLE is far older than 13; what changed in 16 is what it allows.

choices.text: As much as about a superuser
choices.why: Right. It could grant itself the predefined roles that read files and run programs, and the docs of those versions said to treat it as almost a superuser.

prompt: `ALTER ROLE reporting SET statement_timeout = '5min'` is run. bruno, a member of reporting, logs in and starts a report that runs for twenty minutes. What happens?
hint: Which role's settings does a session load?

choices.text: It finishes: the timeout does not reach him
choices.why: Right. Per-role settings apply to the role that logged in, and nobody logs in as reporting.

choices.text: It is cancelled after five minutes
choices.why: That would need the setting on bruno. A setting on a group reaches none of its members.

choices.text: bruno's login is refused until he leaves the group
choices.why: A parameter never decides whether somebody may log in.

choices.text: It is cancelled at once, because a group setting is applied with every SET ROLE
choices.why: bruno never ran SET ROLE, and the setting is read at login anyway.

prompt: After `SET ROLE bruno` in ana's session, what do `current_user` and `session_user` return?
hint: One of them is who logged in.

choices.text: bruno and bruno
choices.why: That is what a real login as bruno shows. SET ROLE does not change who logged in.

choices.text: ana and bruno
choices.why: The other way round: the privileges being checked are bruno's.

choices.text: ana and ana, because SET ROLE only lasts one statement
choices.why: SET ROLE lasts until RESET ROLE or the end of the session.

choices.text: bruno, then ana
choices.why: Right. current_user is whose privileges are checked; session_user is who logged in.

prompt: Match each option of a PostgreSQL 16 membership to the question it answers.
hint: Three options, three questions; one answer belongs to an attribute instead.

pairs.right: Are the group's privileges used without asking?
May the member switch to the group with SET ROLE?
May the member grant the group to others?

right_distractors: May the member log in at all?

prompt: bruno is in reporting `WITH INHERIT FALSE`, and reporting has SELECT on customers. As bruno, `SELECT count(*) FROM customers` is refused. What does he do to read the table?
hint: He is still a member.

choices.text: Ask for `GRANT reporting TO bruno` again, which resets the options
choices.why: A repeated GRANT changes only the options it names; with none named, INHERIT FALSE stays.

choices.text: Run `SET ROLE reporting` first, switching to the group for as long as he needs it
choices.why: Right. Without inheritance, the privilege is reached by becoming the group for a moment.

choices.text: Reconnect, because inheritance applies from the next login
choices.why: INHERIT FALSE is a property of the membership, and a new login does not change it.

choices.text: Nothing: a member without INHERIT has no way to use the privilege
choices.why: SET ROLE is that way, as long as the SET option is on, which is the default.

prompt: To check that bruno cannot become reporting, a colleague runs `SET ROLE bruno; SET ROLE reporting;` from her superuser session, sees `SET` twice, and concludes the SET option is on. What is wrong with the test?
hint: Whose membership does SET ROLE check?

choices.text: Nothing: two SETs prove the option is on
choices.why: In the lesson the option was off and both SETs still worked.

choices.text: She should have used RESET ROLE between the two statements
choices.why: RESET ROLE goes back to ana; the second SET would then test ana, not bruno.

choices.text: The check was made against ana, and she becomes whoever she asks to be
choices.why: Right. Only a real login as bruno makes him the session user, and then the switch is refused.

choices.text: SET ROLE never checks memberships, so the test measures nothing
choices.why: It does check them, against the session user; logged in as bruno it refused.

prompt: psql 16 lists every membership with its options using the backslash command \___.
hint: Three letters, the last one for grants.

prompt: Over the local socket, with Ubuntu's pg_hba.conf, ana runs `psql -U bruno shop`. Why is it refused?
hint: What does peer compare?

choices.text: bruno has no password yet
choices.why: Peer asks for no password at all; it asks the kernel who opened the socket.

choices.text: bruno lacks CONNECT on shop
choices.why: At that point every role had CONNECT through PUBLIC; the message named peer authentication.

choices.text: Her OS user is ana, not bruno
choices.why: Right. Peer lets an operating-system user in as the role with the same name only.

choices.text: Roles created with CREATE USER cannot use the local socket
choices.why: Any role may use the socket; the map later let ana in as bruno through it.

prompt: With `map=shop` on the local line and pg_ident.conf listing only `shop ana bruno`, what happens to ana's ordinary `psql`?
hint: Once a map is on the line, what stops?

choices.text: It is refused
choices.why: Right. Without a line `shop ana ana`, ana has locked herself out of her own role.

choices.text: It still lands as ana, because peer allows matching names anyway
choices.why: With a map, plain name matching stops; only the listed pairs are allowed.

choices.text: It lands as bruno, the only role in the map
choices.why: psql still asks for the role named like you; the map only says whether that is allowed.

choices.text: The server refuses to reload a map with only one line
choices.why: One line is a valid map; the file views report no error for it.

prompt: Put the steps of changing pg_hba.conf safely in order.
hint: Ask the server before you make it act.
items: Copy the file with sudo cp -p
Edit the line with an editor
Read pg_hba_file_rules and look at the error column

prompt: The map lists `shop ana reporting`, and pg_hba.conf accepts the connection. Why is `psql -U reporting shop` still refused?
hint: Two checks, in two places.

choices.text: A map cannot name a group
choices.why: pg_ident_file_mappings showed the line with no error; the map accepted it.

choices.text: The server was not reloaded after the map changed
choices.why: It was, and bruno, from the same map, logged in a moment later.

choices.text: reporting has no LOGIN attribute
choices.why: Right. Authentication says who you are; the role's own attribute says whether that identity may open a session.

choices.text: reporting holds no CONNECT on shop
choices.why: Every role still had CONNECT through PUBLIC, and the message said the role is not permitted to log in.

prompt: What does pg_authid hold for a role whose password was set on PostgreSQL 16 with default settings?
hint: Look at the start of what the query printed.

choices.text: The password, encrypted with a key in postgresql.conf
choices.why: Nothing reversible is stored; there is no key that turns it back into the password.

choices.text: An md5 hash of the password and the role's name
choices.why: That was the default before version 14; password_encryption is scram-sha-256 now.

choices.text: The password in clear text, readable by superusers
choices.why: A superuser can read pg_authid, and what it finds there is a verifier, not the password.

choices.text: A SCRAM verifier: a salted value from which the password cannot be recovered
choices.why: Right. A salted value from 4096 rounds of hashing; the password cannot be read back from it.

prompt: Why did the misspelled `ALTER ROLE brunno PASSWORD '...'` leak bruno's password, when the statement changed nothing?
hint: What does the server write when a statement fails?

choices.text: psql sends every statement to the system journal before running it
choices.why: psql does no such thing. The line was in the server's own log, written by the server.

choices.text: Because brunno was created by the failed statement, with that password
choices.why: ALTER ROLE never creates a role; it answered that brunno does not exist.

choices.text: The server logs a failing statement's text
choices.why: Right. The STATEMENT line carried the password in clear text into the log.

choices.text: It did not leak: an error rolls back the log line too
choices.why: A log is not transactional; tail showed the line after the error.

prompt: A script runs `psql -w -h localhost -U app shop` and fails with `fe_sendauth: no password supplied`, though ~/.pgpass has the right line. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: What did the warning above that line say?

choices.text: The server's pg_hba.conf has no line for localhost
choices.why: Then the server would refuse with its own FATAL; this message is the client giving up before asking.

choices.text: -w makes psql ignore ~/.pgpass
choices.why: -w only forbids prompting; after chmod 600 the same command worked.

choices.text: The file is readable by others
choices.why: Right. libpq ignores a password file with group or world access, and only warns.

choices.text: app's password has expired
choices.why: An expired password fails at the server, with password authentication failed and a DETAIL in the log.

prompt: Which octal mode was given to chmod so that ~/.pgpass is readable by its owner only?
hint: Read and write for the owner, nothing for anybody else.

prompt: app's password has `VALID UNTIL` yesterday. Which of these still works?
hint: VALID UNTIL is about a credential.

choices.text: A new connection over -h localhost with the password from ~/.pgpass
choices.why: That is exactly what failed, with User app has an expired password in the log.

choices.text: A session app opened this morning, before the date passed, and has kept open since
choices.why: Right. The date is checked when a password is presented, and an open session presents none.

choices.text: A new connection with the correct password typed by hand
choices.why: The password was right in the lesson too; it was its date that failed.

choices.text: A new connection after app's password is set again with the same value
choices.why: Setting a password does not clear VALID UNTIL; the date stays until it is changed.

prompt: A deployment tool must create tables as `shop_owner`, but should run every other statement with its own ordinary rights. Which membership fits?
hint: Inherit, or switch on purpose?

choices.text: `GRANT shop_owner TO deployer WITH INHERIT TRUE, SET FALSE`
choices.why: That gives the owner's rights all the time and forbids switching: the opposite of what is asked.

choices.text: `GRANT shop_owner TO deployer WITH INHERIT FALSE`
choices.why: Right. SET stays on by default, so it switches with SET ROLE while it migrates and has nothing extra the rest of the time.

choices.text: `GRANT shop_owner TO deployer WITH ADMIN TRUE`
choices.why: ADMIN lets it hand shop_owner to others, which nobody asked for, and inheritance stays on.

choices.text: `ALTER ROLE deployer SUPERUSER`
choices.why: That removes every check, all the time.

prompt: An application fails to log in, and its log says only `password authentication failed for user "app"`. Where is the actual reason?
hint: The server tells strangers as little as possible.

choices.text: In the server's log, on the DETAIL line written beside the FATAL one
choices.why: Right. The DETAIL there says whether the password was wrong or expired, and which pg_hba.conf line matched.

choices.text: In pg_authid, in a column that records the last failure
choices.why: pg_authid holds no record of attempts; failures go to the log.

choices.text: In the client's message: it has said everything
choices.why: The client gets the same sentence for a wrong password and an expired one, on purpose.

choices.text: In pg_hba_file_rules, whose error column lists refused logins
choices.why: That column reports lines of the file the server cannot parse, not connections.

prompt: Order the checks a connection meets, from first to last, for `psql -h localhost -U bruno shop`.
hint: The file chooses the method before the method runs.
items: The password is checked with scram-sha-256
The role's LOGIN attribute and password date are checked
Privileges are checked statement by statement

prompt: Which of these keep a password out of every file on the server and in your home directory? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about the log, ~/.psql_history and ~/.bash_history.

choices.text: `\password app` in psql
choices.why: Yes. psql sends a verifier; the password is in no statement.

choices.text: `psql -c "ALTER ROLE app PASSWORD 'x'"` at the shell
choices.why: The shell history keeps it, and a failure or log_statement puts it in the server log.

choices.text: `ALTER ROLE app PASSWORD 'x'` typed in interactive psql
choices.why: ~/.psql_history keeps everything typed.

choices.text: A driver that computes the SCRAM verifier and sends it
choices.why: Yes. That is what \password does, done by a program.

prompt: Which psql command shows `Cannot login` beside a role?
hint: The same one that shows Superuser.

choices.text: \drg
choices.why: \drg lists memberships and their options, not attributes.

choices.text: \du
choices.why: Right. It lists roles with their attributes.

choices.text: \dp, the access privileges of every table
choices.why: \dp shows grants on objects; LOGIN is an attribute of the role.

choices.text: \conninfo, which describes the current connection
choices.why: It says who you are connected as, nothing about other roles.
